title: Given the head of a singly linked list, remove the Nth node counting from the end of the list and return the head. Do it in a single pass.
shortTitle: Remove the Nth Node From the End of a Linked List (Two-Pointer With N Gap)
keyPoints: Advance a fast pointer N+1 steps ahead of slow (both starting from a dummy), then move both until fast hits null
The slow pointer lands on the node just before the target, so unlinking is a single reference reassignment
Using a dummy head handles the edge case where the head itself is the node to remove
The algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) space with a single pass through the list
Validate N against the list length to avoid NullPointerException from advancing past the end
The two-pass alternative first counts nodes, then walks to position L-N; both are O(n) but the gap trick is a single pass

s1_definition.oneliner: Move fast N steps ahead, then move both until fast ends, and slow lands right before the node to delete.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Two-pointer gap** – fast pointer leads slow pointer by exactly N+1 nodes so slow stops one node before the target.
- **Dummy head** – a sentinel before the real head so that deleting the first node needs no special case.
- **Unlink** – `slow.next = slow.next.next` removes the target by skipping it in the chain.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space, single pass.
- **Validation** – if N exceeds the list length, fast runs past null and the code must handle that gracefully.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants to cancel the third-from-last scheduled transfer in his pending queue, but the queue has no length counter. A clerk puts one finger on the first slip, then moves a second finger three slips ahead. Both fingers slide forward together until the leading finger falls off the end. The trailing finger is now sitting right before the slip to cancel, so the clerk pulls that slip out and reconnects the chain.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Two-Pointer Gap Technique (n=2)

  Dummy ──> [TRF-001] ──> [TRF-002] ──> [TRF-003] ──> [TRF-004] ──> null

  Step 1: Advance fast by n+1 = 3
  slow = Dummy
  fast = [TRF-003]

  Step 2: Move both until fast = null
  slow = [TRF-002], fast = null

  Step 3: Unlink slow.next (TRF-003)
  Dummy ──> [TRF-001] ──> [TRF-002] ──> [TRF-004] ──> null
```

```text
  Edge Case: Removing Head (n = list length)

  Dummy ──> [A] ──> [B] ──> [C] ──> null
  n = 3, advance fast by 4 steps
  slow = Dummy, fast = null
  Unlink Dummy.next (A)
  Dummy ──> [B] ──> [C] ──> null
  Return Dummy.next = [B]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Removing the Nth node from the end of a singly linked list in one pass uses the two-pointer gap technique. You create a dummy node before the head, advance a fast pointer N+1 steps ahead, then slide both fast and slow forward until fast falls off the end. The gap stays fixed, so slow lands exactly on the node before the target, and you unlink the target with a single `slow.next = slow.next.next`.

The dummy head is what makes this clean. Without it, removing the head node (when N equals the list length) needs a separate code path. With the dummy, every position is handled by the same logic, and you return `dummy.next` at the end.

The advance by N+1 rather than N is a common source of confusion. Both pointers start at the dummy, which is one position before the real head, so the extra step ensures slow ends up one node before the target rather than on the target itself. In a singly linked list you cannot unlink a node you are standing on because you need access to the previous node's `next` pointer.

In production at National Bank of India, Rajesh cancels scheduled transfers by position from the end. The service validates N during the advance phase and returns a safe error if N exceeds the queue length, rather than allowing a `NullPointerException` to crash the request. The gap technique answers in one pass, which matters for long queues under live request latency constraints.

Remember one sentence: advance fast N+1 from dummy, walk both to the end, slow lands before the target, unlink in one step.
